A Shared Redis Connection

config/redis.js — the ioredis connection both the Queue (API process) and the Worker (worker process) are built on.

// Figure 6.1: the shared Redis connection (src/config/redis.js)
import IORedis from 'ioredis';
import env from './env.js';

const connection = new IORedis({
  host: env.REDIS_HOST,
  port: env.REDIS_PORT,
  maxRetriesPerRequest: null,
});

export default connection;

Same import-as-singleton idiom as config/db.js's PrismaClient and config/mailer.js's transport (see Week 5) — one connection object, created once, that every importer shares. What's different here is which processes import it: db.js and mailer.js are only ever imported by the API process. This module is imported by both jobs/slaScan.queue.js (in the API process) and src/worker.js (its own, separate process) — so "singleton" here means one connection per process that imports this module, not one connection for the whole application. Each process ends up with its own TCP connection to Redis, exactly as each would get its own PrismaClient if two processes both imported db.js.

maxRetriesPerRequest: null isn't a style preference — it's BullMQ's own documented requirement. BullMQ issues Redis commands that deliberately block while waiting for a job to arrive; ioredis's default retry behaviour would time those out and retry them, which fights with how BullMQ expects the connection to behave. Every BullMQ connection needs this option set, whether it belongs to a Queue or a Worker.
